Physical therapy usually includes balance training, joint mobility exercises, and muscle strength recovery. Each session is recommended to last 45-60 minutes, and the intensity should be increased gradually based on tolerance. For diet, it is recommended to increase high-quality protein (eggs, fish) and B vitamins while avoiding high salt and fat. It is advised to use a simple scale (such as the Fugl-Meyer motor function score) weekly to record progress. Then I pulled myself together and fully practiced two movements of Baduanjin: 'Holding Both Hands to Lift the Sky and Regulate the Triple Burner' and 'Drawing the Bow Left and Right Like Shooting the Eagle.' The movements were slow and steady, and the 15-minute practice thoroughly stretched the body. Back at home that day, I also helped my father wash up, take his medication, and measure his blood pressure.

Which of these happened first, and which happened later?

For each joint, slowly flex, extend, and rotate 5-10 times within the pain-free range, avoiding excessive stretching and forceful movements. Monitor blood pressure during activity, ensuring systolic pressure <160 mmHg. Coordinating with breathing and soft music works better.

It is recommended to measure and record the joint range of motion before and after activity. In addition, rule out bleeding risk (such as abnormal coagulation function). If your father has hypertension, measure his blood pressure first. You can take weekly photos to record progress.

user.content: My father is 56 years old and has limited mobility after a cerebral infarction. I have booked daily physical therapy at Zhengzhou Jihe Rehabilitation Center starting April 5. I would like to know whether the specific training content, duration, and intensity are suitable for him, and what care and monitoring need to be coordinated at home?

assistant.content: Your father is in the sequelae phase after a cerebral infarction; the golden period for rehabilitation is the first 6 months. Physical therapy usually includes balance training, joint mobility exercises, and muscle strength recovery. Each session is recommended to last 45-60 minutes, and the intensity should be increased gradually based on tolerance. You have already made an appointment with a professional institution; the key is family cooperation: daily assisted standing and walking practice, home modifications to prevent falls, a low-salt and low-fat diet, and monitoring of blood pressure, mood, and whether limb numbness worsens.

user.content: Thank you! So how exactly can we do assisted training at home? Are there any nutrients to supplement in the diet, such as vitamins or protein?

assistant.content: Home-assisted training can be done 3–4 times a day, with 15–20 minutes per session of sit-to-stand exercises, passive range-of-motion exercises for the affected joints (within a pain-free range), and slow walking with support. For diet, it is recommended to increase high-quality protein (eggs, fish) and B vitamins while avoiding high salt and fat. It is advised to use a simple scale (such as the Fugl-Meyer motor function score) weekly to record progress. If dizziness, chest tightness, or other symptoms occur, stop immediately and contact the physician.

Intensity dropped significantly, and frequency changed from every other day to daily but short and low-intensity. This abrupt change directly reflects the shift in life priorities — time, energy, and emotional investment all turned from work, interests, and self-improvement to caring for my father and family responsibilities. assistant.content: During the day, use a spray bottle to evenly mist the towel every 2-3 hours; at night, replace the wet towel with a slightly damp plastic bag over the pottery plate (leave small holes for ventilation) to prevent evaporation from being too fast. Cracking or chipping at turns is usually caused by carving too quickly or using uneven force. Suggestion: slow down before the turn, switch to a finer carving knife (such as a trimming knife) and carve gradually from the inside of the outline toward the outside, letting the wrist drive the blade rather than using force from the arm.

Other recommended exercises: wall sit (strengthens the legs and reduces lower back strain), seated leg raises (no equipment needed), and cat-cow pose (improves spinal flexibility). Do each exercise 8 times first, and increase to 12 times after you adapt.

assistant.content: Suggested base formula: 3-5% iron oxide, 0.5-1% manganese oxide, with transparent or opaque glaze as the base. Apply the glaze twice, each time about 0.5mm thick, and fire at 1230-1260°C in a reducing atmosphere. user.content: How exactly do you operate in a reduction atmosphere? And if I want a warmer, matte finish, should I adjust the temperature or the glaze composition?

assistant.content: A reduction atmosphere is achieved by controlling the oxygen level in the kiln, for example by reducing air intake or adding silicon carbide. If you want a matte, warm finish, you can lower the iron oxide content to 2-3%, add 3-5% zinc oxide or talc, and reduce the firing temperature by 10-20°C. It is recommended to first make 3-5 test pieces for comparison.

answer: In the first half of February (1-7), my exercise was irregular, mainly walking and short stretching. user.content: Yu Xiaowen: When I review my heart failure notes, I'm a bit confused about the preferred choice between ARB and ACEI in different NYHA classes. How should LVEF and symptom weighting be combined with risk stratification? Could you help me sort it out?

assistant.content: Don't worry, this is a commonly tested point. ACEI/ARB are first-line for all HFrEF (LVEF ≤ 40%), recommended for NYHA class II-IV, but ACEIs have stronger evidence (e.g., the SOLVD trial). ARBs are used for ACEI intolerance (e.g., cough, angioedema). Risk stratification is mainly based on NYHA class (symptoms) and LVEF (objective measure): NYHA class III-IV plus LVEF < 35% indicates high risk, requiring consideration of ICD or CRT. Memory aid: ACE first, ARB as backup; LVEF ≤ 40, NYHA determines high risk.

user.content: Yu Xiaowen: Got it. Then in what situations should beta-blockers and aldosterone antagonists be used with caution?

assistant.content: Beta-blockers should be used with caution in acute heart failure, severe bradycardia, and asthma; aldosterone antagonists should be used with caution in hyperkalemia (serum potassium >5.5) and severe renal insufficiency (eGFR <30). When the two are combined, electrolytes and blood pressure need to be monitored. Clinical decision: first use diuretics to reduce edema, then ACEI/ARB plus beta-blockers, then add aldosterone antagonists. This stepwise medication approach is safer and more effective.

question: In February 2025, how did changes in my exercise habits affect the recovery from lower back soreness and the common cold? What role did exercise regularity play in this?

answer: In September 2025, my exercise pattern shifted from indoor static exercise to outdoor morning running. From early to mid-September (6th to 16th), I mainly performed indoor exercises such as Baduanjin and neck exercises, with only one 25-minute outdoor jog attempt on September 10 (at Zhuchunyuan Park), after which I returned to indoor exercise. Starting from September 17, I resumed morning running and gradually made it a regular habit: I ran a total of 7 times on the 17th, 18th, 21st, 23rd, 25th, 28th, and 30th, each run about 3 kilometers, with an average pace of about 7 minutes 30 seconds per kilometer, and heart rate controlled at 130-150 beats per minute, at Bishagang Park or Zhuchunyuan Park. Compared with before, the main changes were: 1) the exercise type changed from indoor static Baduanjin and neck exercises to outdoor dynamic aerobic running; 2) the exercise time was advanced from around 6:30 a.m. to around 5:45 a.m., usually followed by stretching after the run, and on non-running days Baduanjin was still practiced as a supplement; 3) exercise intensity increased from low-intensity joint activity to moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, and heart rate monitoring began to be used to measure exercise intensity.

answer: In early June, I was highly focused on research (e.g., SPSS analysis on June 1-2, the mid-term report on June 3, and writing the first draft of the paper’s methods section on June 9). After meeting with Li Wei on June 20, I postponed the department transfer and turned to preparing for the attending physician exam (mock exam on June 24, intensive review of cardiovascular drugs from June 26 to 30) and developing hobbies (consulting about a hairstyle makeover on June 20, completing the prototype of a tea bowl in pottery class on June 26, choosing a rehabilitation exercise bike on June 28, and completing the hairstyle makeover on June 29). evidence.title: Easily confused points in cardiovascular medicine.
evidence.content:
Differentiation of atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter:
1. ECG features: In atrial fibrillation, P waves disappear and are replaced by f waves (350-600 beats/min), and R-R intervals are absolutely irregular. In atrial flutter, P waves disappear and are replaced by sawtooth-shaped F waves (250-350 beats/min); when the atrioventricular conduction ratio is fixed, R-R intervals are regular.
2. Clinical management: Atrial fibrillation requires ventricular rate control (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers) or anticoagulation (CHA2DS2-VASc score); rhythm control can be electrical cardioversion or medication. For atrial flutter, radiofrequency ablation is the first choice, and electrical cardioversion or drug therapy can also be used to control the ventricular rate.
Excerpted from the evening practice-question analysis on 2025-06-17.

In this case, palpitations and pulse deficit suggest atrial fibrillation, but if the ventricular rate is around 150 beats/min and regular, 2:1 conduction in atrial flutter should be suspected. For management, radiofrequency ablation is the first choice for atrial flutter (success rate >90%); for atrial fibrillation, anticoagulation should be based on the CHA2DS2-VASc score. If Dr. Li's case is confirmed as atrial flutter, cardioversion or ablation should be considered rather than rate control alone. The latest guidelines recommend that synchronized cardioversion is safer when atrial flutter is accompanied by a rapid ventricular rate.

assistant.content: For Plendil (felodipine), the recommended starting dose is 5 mg once daily, the maintenance dose is 5-10 mg once daily, and the maximum dose is 20 mg once daily. Common side effects include headache and peripheral edema (especially ankle), usually dose-related. When used in combination with other antihypertensive drugs (such as beta-blockers), attention should be paid to the risk of hypotension; when used with CYP3A4 inhibitors (such as ketoconazole), the dose should be adjusted. Would you like to know about adjustment plans for a specific patient?

user.content: Yes, I am admitting a 65-year-old female patient with mild abnormal liver function (ALT 60 U/L) and no other medications. Is a starting dose of 5 mg appropriate for her? Are special adjustments needed?

assistant.content: For patients with mild liver function abnormalities, it is recommended to start with 2.5 mg once daily, adjust every 2 weeks based on tolerance and blood pressure response, and a maximum dose of no more than 10 mg. Plendil is mainly metabolized by the liver; hepatic impairment can increase plasma concentration. At the same time, monitoring for ankle edema is recommended, and combination with an ACEI/ARB may be considered to reduce this side effect. If severe headache or hypotension occurs, the drug should be discontinued promptly for evaluation.

question: In April 2025, how did my study focus change from the first half of the month to the second half? What were the main turning points?

answer: My learning in April followed a "dual-track parallel, stage-by-stage progression" pattern. The first track was systematic study of medical statistics: on April 1, I restarted the course and made a catch-up plan, gradually mastering data description, probability distributions, the t-test, and the chi-square test, and passed the completion assessment on April 20. The second track was preparation for the attending physician examination: it began on April 8 after being reminded by my supervising teacher. On the same day, I bought the books and checked the syllabus. On April 14, I made a detailed monthly plan, then started reviewing the cardiovascular system on April 24, and consolidated it through literature reading on April 30. The two tracks were not isolated: in the early period (April 1-7), statistics learning started while exam preparation had not yet begun; in the middle period (April 8-20), the two tracks advanced simultaneously, with intensive statistics learning and exam preparation gradually unfolding; in the later period (April 21-30), statistics was immediately applied to actual work after completing the course (on April 22, analyzing patient satisfaction data; on April 27, writing the methods section of the paper), while exam preparation continued to deepen (e.g., doing practice questions on April 26). In addition, medical humanities reading ran through the whole month, including "Being Mortal", "Better", the literary fiction work "The Night Submarine", and multiple book club discussions (such as co-reading "Lean In", the Wutong Tree Book Club, Fan Deng Co-reading, Nonviolent Communication discussions, and discussions of a women's power reading list), which broadened my clinical perspective. This pattern was closely related to professional development: statistical competence directly serves scientific research papers and clinical data analysis and is the key to academic improvement; preparation for the attending physician examination is a necessary step for professional title promotion and is directly linked to career advancement (during which I also participated in a first aid skills competition to maintain clinical competence); humanities reading strengthens doctor-patient communication and understanding of bioethics, improving overall quality. The three learning tracks jointly point to a growth path that integrates clinical work, research, and the humanities.

user.content: I just finished learning about skewed distributions. The median is more representative of central tendency than the mean, but I don't quite understand the specific reason. Can you explain?

assistant.content: Okay. In a skewed distribution, extreme values significantly pull the mean, while the median is unaffected by extreme values and reflects the central position more stably. Take hospital length of stay, which you are familiar with, as an example: most patients are discharged after a short stay (e.g., 3 days), but a few stay long-term (e.g., 30 days). The mean gets pulled up (e.g., 5.5 days), while the median might be only 3 days, better representing the typical patient's length of stay.

user.content: I see. So in actual research papers, if the data are heavily skewed, should the median be reported instead of the mean?

assistant.content: Yes. A general recommendation is: if the absolute value of the skewness coefficient is greater than 1 or there are obvious outliers in the data, report the median and interquartile range as a priority. In medical research, the median is commonly used for variables such as length of hospital stay, cost, and disease duration. At the same time, combine box plots or histograms to show the distribution shape and enhance persuasiveness.

user.content: I just ran a one-sample t-test in SPSS using case data: the effect of a certain antihypertensive drug on systolic blood pressure. I started with Analyze → Compare Means → One-Sample T Test, but I'm not sure whether the data format needs one row per subject. assistant.content: Your operation steps are correct. The data format is one participant's measurement value per row. Interpreting the results: t=-2.45 indicates the sample mean is lower than the test value; p=0.018 <0.05 rejects H0, so the antihypertensive drug is considered to effectively lower systolic blood pressure. The 95% CI [-5.3, -0.7] indicates that the average reduction ranges from 0.7 to 5.3 mmHg. The conclusion of the paper can be written as: The one-sample t-test showed that after taking the antihypertensive drug, systolic blood pressure was significantly lower than 140 mmHg (t=-2.45, df=29, p=0.018, 95% CI -5.3 to -0.7).

user.content: I see. Do I still need to report the effect size? SPSS doesn't give it directly. How do I calculate it manually?

assistant.content: It is recommended to report Cohen's d = mean difference / standard deviation, reflecting effect size. Formula: d = Mean Difference / SD. In your case, the mean difference is -3; if SD = 6, then d = -0.5, which is a medium effect. In the paper, you can add: Cohen's d = -0.5, indicating moderate clinical significance. In an exam, if the question requires it, you must report it; otherwise, it is optional.

evidence.title: Neurology common mistakes
evidence.content: Localization diagnosis of cerebrovascular disease: middle cerebral artery embolism causes contralateral hemiplegia, contralateral hemisensory disturbance, and contralateral hemianopia (the 'three-hemi' signs); basal ganglia hemorrhage often causes contralateral hemiplegia; brainstem lesions cause crossed paralysis. Parkinson's disease Hoehn-Yahr staging: stage 1, unilateral symptoms; stage 2, bilateral symptoms without balance impairment; stage 3, mild to moderate bilateral symptoms with postural instability; stage 4, severe disability but able to walk independently; stage 5, wheelchair-dependent or bedridden. Differential diagnosis of headache types: migraine (unilateral throbbing, with nausea and vomiting, aggravated by activity); tension-type headache (bilateral pressing, no aura); cluster headache (unilateral sharp, with tearing and nasal congestion, more common at night). Framework of neural pathway diagram: sensory pathways (superficial sensation: spinothalamic tract; deep sensation: medial lemniscus), motor pathways (corticospinal tract, extrapyramidal system, etc.).

question: What directions did my studies mainly focus on in August? What characteristics did the investment pattern have? What is the relationship between these studies and my career transition?

answer:
During August, my interest in rehabilitation medicine deepened from "passive exposure" to "active engagement", specifically reflected in four milestone events:

**Milestone 1: August 5-6 — Submitting the department transfer application**
Driven by both my father's rehabilitation needs and my personal career planning, I drafted the application outline and wrote the handwritten application letter on August 5, and formally submitted it on August 6, marking the shift of my interest from emotional involvement to career decision-making, achieving the transition from "passive exposure" to "active choice".

**Milestone 2: August 11 — Registering for the MOOC course "Basics of Rehabilitation Medicine"**
I formally spent 198 yuan to register for the systematic online course and set a fixed study time every Wednesday and Friday evening, upgrading from fragmented reading to structured learning, reflecting the "systematization" deepening of interest.

**Milestone 3: August 13 — Actively visiting Director Wang Zhenhua of the Rehabilitation Department**
I went to the Department of Rehabilitation Medicine to review materials, and actively visited Director Wang, obtained internal materials, and made an appointment to participate in departmental professional study, marking the leap from "self-study" to "integration into the professional community"; my interest began to acquire social and practical attributes.

**Milestone 4: August 16-31 — In-depth practice and application**
Starting on August 16, I consulted Director Wang again and studied modules such as exercise therapy in depth. On August 18, I completed the neurorehabilitation module test and scored 86 points; on August 27, I prepared a poster; on August 28, I attended the opening ceremony and special reports of the rehabilitation annual conference, and presented my poster during the exchange session; on August 31, I applied the knowledge to my father's rehabilitation training, and also carried out volunteer service at a nursing home with friends, guiding elderly hemiplegic patients in rehabilitation. Together, these activities show that my interest reached the level of "practice and application".

In summary, the path of deepening interest was: vague interest triggered by family caregiving → career direction decision → knowledge accumulation from systematic courses → integration into professional social circles → implementation of practical application. Each step was supported by clear events and intrinsic motivations.

user.content: Today's checkup found hemoglobin 105, mild iron-deficiency anemia, and a body fat rate of 24%. Recently I have occasionally felt dizzy and fatigued. I bought iron-supplementing foods such as pork liver and beef myself, but I am not sure how to combine them more scientifically, and I am also worried that the exercise intensity may be wrong. Can you give me a systematic adjustment plan?

assistant.content: It is recommended to prioritize iron supplementation combined with vitamin C, such as pork liver or lean beef stir-fried with green peppers and tomatoes, and eating oranges or kiwifruit after meals. At the same time, avoid strong tea and coffee, which interfere with absorption. For exercise, focus on low-intensity aerobic activities such as walking and yoga, keeping heart rate at (220 - age) × 60%-70%, for 20-30 minutes each session. Recheck the complete blood count after 2 weeks; if hemoglobin has not improved, consider iron supplementation.

user.content: I've remembered the vitamin C combination. During exercise, how do I judge whether the intensity is appropriate? If I need to take iron supplements, should I consult a doctor first?

assistant.content: When exercising, use being able to speak normally without panting as the standard, and avoid holding your breath or jumping movements. For iron supplementation, it is recommended to consult a doctor first, because soluble iron may cause gastrointestinal discomfort and the dose needs to be determined. A body fat rate of 24% is normal on the high side. As anemia improves, gradually increase aerobic duration, but in the early stage, focus on restoring physical strength.

user.content: My father is 56 years old, a retired teacher, and his lower back isn't great. I found a few low-difficulty core activation exercise videos and want to send them to him to practice over the weekend. Are these exercises safe? What should I be careful about?

assistant.content: Low-intensity core activation exercises are generally suitable for people aged 56 without a serious medical history, but it is still necessary to assess whether your father has back pain, hypertension, or osteoporosis. It is recommended to first have him do a 5-minute warm-up (such as joint movements), keep breathing even during exercise, and avoid holding his breath. Start with a small range of motion and gradually increase it. 8-10 repetitions per set, 2-3 sets per day is enough. If lower back pain worsens during exercise, stop immediately.

user.content: I see. My father has mild hypertension, but no severe lower back pain. Do these movements need to be coordinated with breathing? Are there any other suitable home training exercises for him?

assistant.content: If you have high blood pressure, avoid movements in which the head is lower than the heart (such as a bowing posture), and stand up slowly. Breathing advice: exhale during exertion, inhale when returning to the starting position. Other recommended exercises: wall sit (strengthens the legs and reduces lower back strain), seated leg raises (no equipment needed), and cat-cow pose (improves spinal flexibility). Do each exercise 8 times first, and increase to 12 times after you adapt.

user.content: I was recently diagnosed with mild iron-deficiency anemia and have started taking ferrous sulfate tablets. I'd like detailed advice on follow-up management, such as how to assess the treatment effect, what dietary precautions to take, and how soon I can resume morning jogging.

assistant.content: Your main concerns are the standard methods of iron supplementation treatment, avoiding side effects, and when you can safely resume moderate-intensity exercise, right?

user.content: Yes, especially the dietary restrictions and the timing for returning to exercise.

assistant.content: Ferrous sulfate is recommended to be taken after meals with orange juice to reduce gastrointestinal irritation; avoid taking it with milk, calcium tablets, or high-fiber foods. After rechecking ferritin to the normal range (15-150 ng/mL), you can resume brisk walking first, and if your heart rate remains normal, gradually transition to jogging. Seek medical attention promptly if severe constipation or stomach pain occurs.

user.content: I just wrote tomorrow's breakfast plan: boiled eggs and oatmeal with milk, but I realized that the calcium in milk may affect the iron supplement I will start taking tonight (ferrous sulfate tablets). How should I arrange the timing or adjust breakfast to ensure the medicine works?

assistant.content: I understand your concern. Calcium does inhibit iron absorption, so it's recommended to take milk and iron supplements at least 2 hours apart. You could consider taking the medication two hours after breakfast, and take it with orange juice (vitamin C promotes absorption). Keep eggs and oatmeal for breakfast, and move the milk to lunch or afternoon.

user.content: Then tomorrow morning I'll have breakfast at 8, take the medicine and drink orange juice at 10, is that okay? I'll move the milk to noon. Also, I felt good after the first dose. Should I continue taking the medicine with orange juice tomorrow?

assistant.content: Completely feasible. Have breakfast at 8:00 (eggs + oatmeal, avoiding dairy), take the iron tablet with half a glass of orange juice at 10:00, and drink milk at lunch. I suggest you set a medication reminder for 9:55 tomorrow morning right now so you don't forget. Continuing with orange juice is a good habit; vitamin C significantly improves iron absorption.

user.content: Today I started my anemia diet plan, ate spinach and pork liver porridge and took an iron supplement, and also made a morning jog recovery plan. I want to confirm whether the combination of diet and iron supplement is reasonable, and the safety of transitioning from brisk walking to jogging.

assistant.content: As a doctor, you want science-based advice. Taking iron supplements with vitamin C can improve absorption, but avoid taking them with tea or coffee. Starting your morning jog recovery plan with brisk walking is safe, but I recommend monitoring your heart rate, targeting 60%-70% of your maximum heart rate. Do you need me to explain the heart rate calculation formula and how to deal with iron supplement side effects in detail?

user.content: Yes, I'm worried that the iron supplement may cause gastrointestinal discomfort, and about the pressure on my knees during morning runs. Also, I've taken a fancy to a pair of Asics running shoes, but I'm not sure if the arch type is suitable.

assistant.content: Iron supplements should be taken after meals to reduce gastrointestinal reactions; black stools are normal. Warming up fully before morning runs (e.g., dynamic stretching) and choosing running shoes with good cushioning can prevent knee pain. If your Asics running shoes are the apricot pink model, it is recommended to confirm your arch type — normal arches can choose the cushioning series, while low arches need the stability series. You can photograph the wet footprint of your arch and send it to me to help determine.

user.content: After following the anemia diet plan for a week, I feel less sleepy in the afternoon, and I tolerate the iron supplement well. I'd like to further optimize iron absorption. Any suggestions?

assistant.content: That's a good result! To promote iron absorption, I suggest taking your iron supplement with vitamin C, such as kiwi or orange; at the same time, avoid taking it with milk or coffee, preferably with a 1-2 hour interval. Are you currently taking the iron supplement in the morning?

user.content: Yes, I took it with milk this morning. It seems I need to adjust the timing. Also, I want to add leafy green vegetables—which one is better for iron supplementation?

assistant.content: It is recommended to separate the iron supplement and milk; it can be taken on an empty stomach or with orange juice. For leafy greens, spinach and kale are recommended, but they contain oxalic acid and should be blanched before eating. You can also eat red meat or animal liver once or twice a week, and have your hemoglobin checked regularly. Over the long term, you can keep walking after meals and avoid strenuous exercise. Keep recording—you're doing well!

user.content: This is my first morning run today—3 km in 28 minutes, heart rate 130-140, cadence 160, and it felt okay. Are these numbers reasonable?

assistant.content: This pace is about 9 minutes 20 seconds per kilometer, which is very suitable for beginners. The heart rate is in the 65%–75% range of maximum heart rate, making it aerobic base training. The cadence is a bit low; it is recommended to increase it to 170–180 steps per minute to reduce the risk of injury.

user.content: Then how should the cadence be adjusted? And what heart rate range should be maintained?

assistant.content: Cadence can be trained with a metronome or music rhythm, gradually increasing from the current 160 to 170. For heart rate, it is recommended to maintain 130-140 initially; after adaptation, you can try 140-150. Be sure to complete the post-run stretching, and increase weekly distance by no more than 10%.

user.content: Okay, my colleague reminded me to replenish electrolytes. Do I need to specifically drink a sports drink?

assistant.content: A 3 km morning run doesn't produce much sweat; plain boiled water with a little salt is enough. If the weather is hot or the distance extends beyond 5 km, consider an electrolyte drink. Before a morning run, it's recommended to drink 200 ml of warm water and eat a banana afterward.

user.content: My father is 56 years old and has limited mobility after a cerebral infarction. I have booked daily physical therapy at Zhengzhou Jihe Rehabilitation Center starting April 5. I would like to know whether the specific training content, duration, and intensity are suitable for him, and what care and monitoring need to be coordinated at home?

assistant.content: Your father is in the sequelae phase after a cerebral infarction; the golden period for rehabilitation is the first 6 months. Physical therapy usually includes balance training, joint mobility exercises, and muscle strength recovery. Each session is recommended to last 45-60 minutes, and the intensity should be increased gradually based on tolerance. You have already made an appointment with a professional institution; the key is family cooperation: daily assisted standing and walking practice, home modifications to prevent falls, a low-salt and low-fat diet, and monitoring of blood pressure, mood, and whether limb numbness worsens.

user.content: Thank you! So how exactly can we do assisted training at home? Are there any nutrients to supplement in the diet, such as vitamins or protein?

assistant.content: Home-assisted training can be done 3–4 times a day, with 15–20 minutes per session of sit-to-stand exercises, passive range-of-motion exercises for the affected joints (within a pain-free range), and slow walking with support. For diet, it is recommended to increase high-quality protein (eggs, fish) and B vitamins while avoiding high salt and fat. It is advised to use a simple scale (such as the Fugl-Meyer motor function score) weekly to record progress. If dizziness, chest tightness, or other symptoms occur, stop immediately and contact the physician.

user.content: Today I succeeded in asking the director to reduce my night shifts from twice a week to once. In the evening, I also performed a remote memorial ritual at home facing the direction of Luoyang, lighting a ceramic lamp I had made myself and writing a prayer note. I feel a bit complicated - reassured, yet also worried about my father's recovery.

assistant.content: It sounds like you did two very important things today—striving for something at work and an emotional ritual. I can feel how much you care about your father's recovery and the calm after giving it your all. You want to confirm that these efforts are meaningful, right?

user.content: Yes, I'm worried about my father's condition after surgery, but with fewer night shifts, I can spend more time video chatting with him in the evenings. The ritual makes me feel that my grandparents are also blessing him. I just don't know if doing this is enough.

assistant.content: You have already balanced work and family to the best of your ability, and through rituals you have conveyed love and longing to your family — that in itself is a kind of strength. Your father feels your heartfelt intention, and it also nourishes your own heart. These efforts are absolutely worth it, so please give yourself some affirmation.

user.content: Today I accompanied my father to Jian'an Community Rehabilitation Center for ankle pump, seated leg raises, and resistance band training. I wrote down the key points of the movements, but I'm not sure they're accurate, such as the timing of force for ankle pumps and the knee angle for seated leg raises. Could you help me verify them?

assistant.content: You are worried that an error in the records might affect the safety of your father's rehabilitation, so you need to confirm the key points of exertion, the number of sets and frequency, and the subsequent progression plan. Please describe the movement details you recorded; I will double-check them and add any contraindications.

user.content: What I remember is: ankle pump, 3 sets a day, 20 reps per set, toes pointed up for 5 seconds then press down; seated leg raises require the thigh parallel to the ground, knee slightly bent and not locked, 10 reps per side for 3 sets; resistance band training is seated abduction, pull to the maximum position and hold for 3 seconds each time. Right? Also, my father practiced for 1 hour today and is a bit tired. When should I increase the difficulty?

assistant.content: Your records are basically correct: the ankle pump should be held for 5-10 seconds, avoiding rapid twitching. For seated leg lifts, the knee slightly bent is correct, but you need to make sure the lower back stays pressed against the sofa back. During elastic band abduction, be careful not to shrug the shoulders. It is recommended that the total daily amount not exceed 3 sets, and fatigue should be judged by whether your father can complete the moves and has no soreness the next day. Progression: after completing the current number of sets easily for one week, you can increase the exercise time or the number of sets by 15%. Diet: increase intake of high-quality protein (fish, eggs) and calcium. At the follow-up visit, record the number of sets your father completed and his fatigue response so the therapist can adjust accordingly.

user.content: Great, I've remembered these details. Also, my father has high blood pressure. Should he pay attention to breathing rhythm when doing these movements? For example, is holding his breath risky?

assistant.content: Important reminder: For hypertensive patients, rehabilitation training must avoid breath-holding, as it can cause a sudden spike in blood pressure. Every movement should be coordinated with exhaling on exertion (e.g., exhale when lifting the leg, inhale when lowering it), with a steady rhythm. If your father experiences dizziness, chest tightness, or blood pressure fluctuations, stop immediately and rest. user.content: I just finished learning about skewed distributions. The median is more representative of central tendency than the mean, but I don't quite understand the specific reason. Can you explain?

assistant.content: Okay. In a skewed distribution, extreme values significantly pull the mean, while the median is unaffected by extreme values and reflects the central position more stably. Take hospital length of stay, which you are familiar with, as an example: most patients are discharged after a short stay (e.g., 3 days), but a few stay long-term (e.g., 30 days). The mean gets pulled up (e.g., 5.5 days), while the median might be only 3 days, better representing the typical patient's length of stay.

user.content: I see. So in actual research papers, if the data are heavily skewed, should the median be reported instead of the mean?

assistant.content: Yes. A general recommendation is: if the absolute value of the skewness coefficient is greater than 1 or there are obvious outliers in the data, report the median and interquartile range as a priority. In medical research, the median is commonly used for variables such as length of hospital stay, cost, and disease duration. At the same time, combine box plots or histograms to show the distribution shape and enhance persuasiveness.

user.content: I'm writing a paper on orthopedic rehabilitation and need to use propensity score matching (PSM) to balance baseline data. Can you first briefly explain its principles and applicable scenarios?

assistant.content: PSM is a method for eliminating confounding bias in non-randomized studies. It uses logistic regression to calculate the probability of each sample receiving treatment (the propensity score), then matches the treatment group and control group based on the scores. It is suitable for observational studies or retrospective data, for example, comparing the effects of two surgical approaches. The difference from logistic regression is that PSM matches first and then analyzes, while logistic regression directly controls covariates.

user.content: Got it. Then how can I quickly implement PSM in SPSS? Also, I have data from several previous papers and need to do a comparative analysis with them. Do you have any strategies?

assistant.content: In SPSS, you can use the PS Matching extension plug-in (needs to be downloaded). Steps: 1) Define matching variables and exact matching criteria; 2) Set the caliper value (0.02-0.05); 3) Perform matching and check balance. For literature comparison, it is suggested to first unify inclusion criteria and outcome indicators, and use a forest plot to show the similarities and differences in effect sizes. In the discussion section, focus on explaining reasons for differences (such as population, follow-up time, and methodology). When submitting, pay attention to the target journal's requirements for word count (usually 5,000-8,000 words) and figure/table formats. The Cover Letter should emphasize innovation and clinical significance.
